title: Wonderland
full_review:
"Wonderland" (Lions Gate) tells the fact-based story of porn-star John Holmes' involvement in a grisly quadruple homicide, which took place in the Laurel Canyon neighborhood of Los Angeles in 1981. Full of graphically disturbing violence, director James Cox sets out to explore a morally barren landscape so devoid of redeemable features that it is nearly impossible for viewers to invest any emotional interest, let alone sympathy, in the film's mostly repellent characters.

Told in "Roshomon" fashion, the visually self-conscious film weaves together multiple points of view of the events leading up to the brutal slayings. In each, Holmes (played by Val Kilmer), whose implication in the crime elevated it from run-of-the-mill tragedy to a three-ring tabloid circus, remains the central figure.

When the action takes up, Holmes' smutty star has already fallen. Still clinging to his slimy sex-industry laurels, Holmes, a washed-up junkie desperate for cash and cocaine, is forced to slither from one party to the next in order to score his next hit. Riding shotgun on his spiraling-out-of-control tour of dopeville's seedy motels and drug dens is Dawn Schiller (Kate Bosworth), Holmes' underage, strung-out girlfriend, who, along with his estranged ex-wife (Lisa Kudrow), form the narrative's dysfunctional love triangle.

Amid the bottom feeders, Holmes befriends Ron Launius (Josh Lucas), a loose-cannon dealer, and his "business partner," David Lind (Dylan McDermott), a tattooed biker and stone-cold killer. While partying at Ron's haunt, high -- literally and figuratively -- above the eponymous Wonderland Avenue, Holmes ill-advisedly suggests that they rob the sybaritic pleasure palace of his friend, Eddie Nash (Eric Bogosian), a notorious L.A. club owner with a fearsome reputation for viciousness.

With Holmes working from the inside, the robbery goes smoothly, netting the Wonderland gang $250,000 in drugs and loot. Shortly afterward, Nash retaliates, ordering the gruesome Wonderland massacre in which Ron, an accomplice and two of the crews' girlfriends are bludgeoned to death with lead pipes; another victim (Christina Applegate) survives the bloodbath, but suffers brain damage. Lind, fearing for his life, turns himself in to the authorities and spills the beans about the robbery. He also rats out Holmes, who may have played both sides against the middle in order to save his own skin.

Much of Kilmer's performance, which roller-coasters between cocaine-rush highs and lows, seems to be a retread from his last foray into self-destructive hedonism as rock star Jim Morrison in Oliver Stone's 1991 "The Doors." Like Stone's pretentious opus, "Wonderland" fails to achieve the sense of cultural importance it desperately seeks.

Why should anyone really care about Holmes, who comes across as nothing more than a pathetic, self-indulgent loser? As a character, he lacks any traits worthy of empathy or warranting interest. Perhaps the screens of text which bookend the film offer the clearest, self-incriminating argument against the lifestyle depicted. The first boasts that Holmes made more than 1,000 pornographic movies and slept with more than 14,000 women. The film closes with a coda stating that in 1988, at age 44, John Holmes died of AIDS.

While steering clear of adulation, the film does attempt to paint Holmes as a tragic figure worthy of compassion if not sympathy -- which is more than is allowed the film's only "religious" character. In a cameo role, Carrie Fisher plays a Christian woman who reaches out to Dawn in an attempt to rescue her from her dead-end existence. Dawn repays the woman's kindness by snorting cocaine and having sex with Holmes in her bathroom amid devotional pictures of the Blessed Virgin. Upon discovering them, the woman throws them out of her house ranting stereotypical holy-roller chastisements worthy of Dana Carvey's Church Lady.

What is most disturbing about the film is not that it chooses to explore such morally bleak territory, but that in doing so it fails to shed any redemptive light on the darkness. Cox seems content to limit his depressing palette to just two colors -- black and pitch black. In opting for a canvas so bereft of humanity -- let alone hope -- the story is stripped of its cautionary merits. This of course should be of little concern to the filmmaker, who seems more intent on exploiting the sleazy tabloid angles of sex and murder than on actually offering any insights into the tragic events or lives depicted.

Anything but wonderful, "Wonderland" isn't worth the visit.

Due to excessive graphic violence, sexual encounters with partial nudity, recurring drug abuse, and much rough and crude language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
